chapter: Teschemacher, Pee Wee, Noon and Simeon
title: Jimmie Noone's technique and why his influence stopped short of hot playing
summary: Pee Wee tried to imitate Noone's records; Chace admires Noone's time and register changes but says he did not crackle.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Bud Jacobson told me once that he knew Pee-wee in the late 20s, and that Pee-wee would listen to a record of Jimmy Noon's with his Apex Club Orchestra. I know that you know, which, of course, as everybody knows, has enormously fleet, low register work on it. And Pee-wee tried to imitate the choruses, every note. Now, in that connection, we know this much that Pee-wee deliberately tried to imitate Noon. All I can say is I'm very happy that he failed. I like Noon's work enormously, but I would much less rather have two Noons than I would have what we have Pee-wee Russell playing today.

Noon, in some respects, was superficial, and there was so much embroidery to his playing that sometimes either the melodic content or the hot content or the rhythm got lost in frills. Now, the frills generally were well-
He can be accused of that, I think.
They were not, but sometimes the embroidery was just too much.

I think so. Aesthetically speaking, yes, but it remains that Noon is a model for clarinet players, I think. His time was excellent. His tone was unique. He had a beautiful grace in his playing. Now, however fast...
You may also have shown how the change of register is...

Well, yes, that's very important. The quick moving between the registers, the staccato, octave and similar intervals. Yeah, and I hope that that influence isn't waning. Nobody much is doing it. And it should be done with restraint and discretion, of course.
Actually, you made two instruments out of it. It was a solo instrument in two ranges. Yeah. It's true. But speaking about...
We finish up on Noon, maybe. I don't think that he can be regarded as much of a progenitor of the hot Chicago style, because he didn't crackle.

He tried, but he played too easily for that. He had too much serenity about his playing. The younger white Chicago guys had something else in mind. They admired Noon's technique, and they learned all they could from it, and the bending of the notes and everything, but... Noon's influence stopped at the point of hot playing, and we were talking earlier, John, about Omer Simeon, and I was wondering if Omer Simeon wasn't a more important influence on the younger white Chicago players. I don't know.
